nodes.label: Michel de Certeau
nodes.date_label: 1970 La Possession de Loudun — selected and presented historical texts · 1975 L’écriture de l’histoire · 1980 L’invention du quotidien, 1
nodes.description: Michel de Certeau joined historical research on religion and mysticism to questions about how histories are written and how people use cultural forms. La Possession de Loudun presents selected historical texts; L’écriture de l’histoire examines historical practice. In The Practice of Everyday Life, he investigates situated ways of operating within imposed systems. His account of users’ creative activities also questions explanations concerned chiefly with disciplinary power. The English preface distinguishes his volume from Luce Giard and Pierre Mayol’s companion work on dwelling and cooking.

nodes.label: Charles Tilly
nodes.date_label: 1964 The Vendée · 1985 War Making and State Making as Organized Crime · 1986 The Contentious French
nodes.description: Charles Tilly combined historical sociology with research on collective action, revolution and state formation. His studies range from counterrevolution in the Vendée to changing French political repertoires and comparisons across European states. In his essay on war making, coercion and extraction help explain the growth of state organizations, while resistance and bargaining constrain rulers. These are historically situated arguments; he explicitly rejects treating early modern Europe as a ready-made forecast for twentieth-century societies.

nodes.label: Timothy Mitchell
nodes.date_label: 1988 Colonising Egypt · 1991 Colonising Egypt — paperback with new preface · 2002 Rule of Experts
nodes.description: Timothy Mitchell investigates colonial power through the organization of space, knowledge and everyday administration. Colonising Egypt studies nineteenth-century arrangements that made populations and places appear ordered and governable. He connects disciplinary practices to colonial settings rather than treating them as developments confined to Europe. Rule of Experts and Carbon Democracy extend his historical inquiries into expertise, political economy and energy. His work combines historical research with political theory; the selected connections here rest on his own paperback preface to Colonising Egypt.

nodes.label: Jack Goody
nodes.date_label: 1963 With Ian Watt, The Consequences of Literacy · 1983 The Development of the Family and Marriage in Europe · 2006 The Theft of History
nodes.description: Jack Goody brought anthropological comparison to histories of kinship, literacy and Eurasian societies. His jointly authored work with Ian Watt examined literacy; The Development of the Family and Marriage in Europe questioned claims about uniquely European family patterns while distinguishing kinship from demographic measures. The Theft of History criticizes accounts that make European experience the template for universal historical development. His comparisons seek similarities and differences across societies; they do not establish a single timeless family system or an undifferentiated East.

nodes.label: Tzvetan Todorov
nodes.date_label: 1982 La Conquête de l’Amérique · 1984 The Conquest of America — Richard Howard’s English translation · 1991 Face à l’extrême
nodes.description: Tzvetan Todorov connected literary and semiotic inquiry with historical questions about conquest, moral choice and collective memory. La Conquête de l’Amérique uses the encounter between Europeans and Americans to examine relations with others; his short 1984 essay explicitly chooses Mexico as its historical case. Later works address extreme violence and wartime France. In his own essay on memory, commemoration does not automatically prevent renewed violence: narratives of past victimhood can also legitimate aggression. These selected arguments retain their ethical and interpretive character.

nodes.label: Partha Chatterjee
nodes.date_label: 1986 Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World · 1993 The Nation and Its Fragments · 2012 The Black Hole of Empire
nodes.description: Partha Chatterjee studies colonial nationalism and the changing practices of imperial power. His work joins political theory and anthropology to historical research on colonial and postcolonial India. In his interview about The Black Hole of Empire, he explains how a local story of Calcutta and its memorial becomes the spine of a wider inquiry into concepts and practices of empire. He also identifies a lesson from Subaltern Studies: popular cultural forms can be analysed alongside elite political discourse. These are selective historical methods rather than a claim that one account exhausts empire.

nodes.label: Alessandro Portelli
nodes.date_label: 1981 The Peculiarities of Oral History · 1991 The Death of Luigi Trastulli and Other Stories · 1997 The Battle of Valle Giulia
nodes.description: Alessandro Portelli examines oral testimony as an encounter that produces historical evidence. His studies of Italian workers and other communities distinguish the chronology of events from the meanings narrators give them. In his methodological essay, voice, rhythm and narrative form matter, while an interview’s questions and circumstances help shape its answers. Errors in a remembered date can therefore become evidence about memory without replacing the established event chronology. His work combines oral history with literature and music scholarship.

nodes.label: Alexis de Tocqueville
nodes.date_label: 1835 De la démocratie en Amérique — first part · 1840 De la démocratie en Amérique — second part · 1856 L’Ancien Régime et la Révolution
nodes.description: Alexis de Tocqueville investigated democratic society and the historical conditions of revolutionary change while also writing and acting as a political thinker. De la démocratie en Amérique appeared in two parts; L’Ancien Régime et la Révolution returned to prerevolutionary France. In its preface he explains his use of cahiers, provincial records and administrative archives, asking how practices and social relations survived apparent rupture. His study is an earlier historical inquiry into power and society, not membership in a twentieth-century historiographical school.

nodes.label: Steven Hahn
nodes.date_label: 1983 The Roots of Southern Populism · 2003 A Nation Under Our Feet · 2009 The Political Worlds of Slavery and Freedom
nodes.description: Steven Hahn reconstructs popular politics in the United States through slavery, emancipation, rural society and the changing nation. The Roots of Southern Populism and A Nation Under Our Feet place farmers and Black political actors within wider transformations. In his discussion of The Political Worlds of Slavery and Freedom, he challenges accounts that make assimilation into citizenship the sole destination of Black politics. He also asks historians to recognize enslaved people’s wartime flight and armed participation as political action. This identity is distinct from Steven C. Hahn, the historian of Creek and Mary Musgrove histories.

edges.relationship: Situated ways of operating become objects of historical and cultural inquiry
edges.evidence_note: English preface ix and General Introduction xi–xii examine relational practices and refuse an atomistic model of the user; this is a bounded methodological contribution.

edges.relationship: Cultural consumption can transform the uses of imposed representations
edges.evidence_note: General Introduction xii–xiv distinguishes representations and purchase/attendance statistics from what users make with cultural products. This does not establish that every consumer resists power.

edges.relationship: Questions an account of discipline centred on the apparatus that produces it
edges.evidence_note: General Introduction xiv–xv directly discusses Discipline and Punish and asks how users appropriate or evade disciplinary arrangements. This specific criticism preserves the acknowledged analytical debt.

edges.relationship: War finance and organized coercion help shape European state formation
edges.evidence_note: Primary chapter 169–172 links warfare, resource extraction and capital accumulation; analogy with protection rackets is an argument, not a claim that every state is identical to a criminal organization.

edges.relationship: Coercion and bargaining are analysed as historically variable processes
edges.evidence_note: Primary chapter 169–170 says popular resistance could force rulers to concede protection and constraints, and rejects direct future-from-European-past extrapolation. This scoped mechanism claim supplies no universal historical sequence.

edges.relationship: Colonial power is examined through the production of ordered spaces and governable persons
edges.evidence_note: Paperback preface ix–xi describes rural regulation, schooling and spatial partition; its historical claim concerns the power to colonise rather than a comprehensive narrative of British occupation.

edges.relationship: Spatial organization becomes part of an inquiry into governing power
edges.evidence_note: Preface x–xii links surveillance, enclosure and exhibitionary order with colonial power, and locates disciplinary experiments beyond Europe. The connection concerns this documented analysis, not universal adoption by spatial historians.

edges.relationship: Questions the uniqueness and uniformity of European family patterns
edges.evidence_note: Primary 8–9 distinguishes kinship questions from demographic measures, stresses regional/social variation and considers Tibet/Roman Egypt counterexamples. The cited studies themselves were not independently checked.

edges.relationship: Challenges Europe-centred templates for world historical comparison
edges.evidence_note: Introduction 1–3 criticizes projecting European categories onto other societies and asks why Eurasian similarities disappear from divergence narratives. His argument is represented as a comparative challenge, not a proven global consensus.

edges.relationship: Uses conquest as a historical case for examining attitudes toward other societies
edges.evidence_note: The three authored opening paragraphs of “The Morality of Conquest, ” printed 89, explicitly identify the conquest of Mexico and its texts as the case. This limited methodological connection does not assert the unread book’s full thesis or label Todorov a member of a later school.

edges.relationship: Challenges the assumption that remembering victimhood necessarily prevents violence
edges.evidence_note: Own UNESCO essay distinguishes selective remembrance from ethical use and warns that former victims can become aggressors. This is his bounded intervention on public memory, not a psychological finding or a universal judgment on victims.

edges.relationship: Braids a local imperial narrative with the history of governing concepts and practices
edges.evidence_note: The 2012 interview at 2–3 explains how Fort William and the Black Hole story connect with selectively traced political economy, law and techniques of imperial power. Chatterjee explicitly notes that selection was necessary; no exhaustive global history is inferred.

edges.relationship: Brings popular cultural practices into the historical analysis of imperial power
edges.evidence_note: At 2, Chatterjee says he learned through Subaltern Studies to interrogate popular culture theoretically. Theatre and football enter alongside policy and elite discourse. His sweeping claim about what other intellectual historians omit is not adopted.

edges.relationship: Treats the interview as evidence produced through a relationship
edges.evidence_note: The adapted 1991 excerpt, section IV, describes questions, changing relationships and the distortion caused by removing the interviewer’s voice. The handout modernizes bracketed terms and is not an exact 1981 transcription.

edges.relationship: Uses displaced chronology to examine narrated meaning without changing event dates
edges.evidence_note: The adapted excerpt, section III, uses workers’ memories of Trastulli in Terni to distinguish event chronology from narrated meaning. Factual verification remains necessary; false memories do not replace established dates.

edges.relationship: Investigates administrative continuity across revolutionary rupture
edges.evidence_note: The 1856 Avant-propos at 5–12 asks how habits and institutions from the monarchy persisted after 1789. This is an earlier historical inquiry into political change, not membership in a modern school.

edges.relationship: Uses administrative archives to investigate relations among classes and everyday governance
edges.evidence_note: At 7–10, Tocqueville describes moving beyond celebrated writers and public figures toward institutional practices, relations among classes and provincial administrative archives. This is his research programme; it does not make every archival voice representative.

edges.relationship: Questions a slavery-to-freedom narrative centred only on integration and citizenship
edges.evidence_note: Nichols’s 2009 feature quotes Hahn challenging a narrative centred on integration and citizenship, and describes aspirations outside that framework. This connection concerns that documented intervention, not all African American historical experience.

edges.relationship: Interprets enslaved people’s wartime flight and armed participation as political action
edges.evidence_note: The 2009 feature and direct book quotation describe Hahn’s interpretation of enslaved people’s wartime flight and armed participation as rebellion. The interpretation remains attributed to him; no uncontested ranking of the largest rebellion is asserted.
